analysis.one_liner: Requires large trucks to have speed limiters set at 65 mph.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Commerce Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Department of Transportation to issue rules within one year requiring all new large trucks (over 26,000 pounds) to be equipped with technology that caps their speed at 65 miles per hour, or 70 mph if the truck also has automatic emergency braking and adaptive cruise control. It would also require trucks built after 1992 that already have limiters installed to actually use them. The bill cites federal data that 10,440 people died in crashes from 2004 to 2013 where truck speed likely made the crash worse.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who shares the road with large trucks. The bill's own findings cite a federal study finding that trucks without speed limiters had a speed-related crash rate almost twice as high as trucks using them, and a truck-driver survey in which 64 percent favored requiring limiters. It also cited Australia, the UK, and the EU, which have required speed limiters on trucks since the 1990s.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, passengers, and cyclists sharing roads with trucks

how_it_helps.text: Cites federal data that 10,440 people died in crashes between 2004 and 2013 in which the speed of a commercial truck likely contributed to the severity, and directs the government to act on it.
Cites a federal study finding trucks without speed-limiting technology had a speed-related crash rate almost twice as high as trucks using it.

Would have required new rules within one year: speed limiters on all new large trucks capped at 65 mph (70 mph with automatic braking and adaptive cruise control), and mandatory use of limiters already installed in trucks built after 1992.
Cited a survey of truck drivers in which 64 percent supported a speed-limiting requirement, meaning much of the workforce directly affected did not oppose it.

analysis.who_pays: Motor carriers, mainly through slower maximum speeds that can lengthen delivery times, and through the cost of equipping trucks that lack limiters and certifying compliance to the Secretary of Transportation. Small operators with older trucks that have no limiter installed would face the equipment cost; large fleets that already limit their trucks' speed would face little new cost.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have required every truck owner to verify and certify compliance to the Department of Transportation, adding a paperwork and enforcement burden, and carriers would bear the cost of equipping any truck without a limiter.

A 65 mph cap creates a speed gap between trucks and cars on highways posted at 70 mph or higher, an argument opponents raise because vehicles moving at very different speeds must interact; the bill partially addressed this by allowing 70 mph for trucks with automatic braking and adaptive cruise control.
Slower truck speeds can lengthen shipping times and add operating costs, which can ultimately show up in freight prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case in the bill's own findings is strong: a federal study showing roughly double the crash rate for trucks without limiters, more than 10,000 deaths over a decade in speed-related truck crashes, driver support in a major survey, and two decades of use in other wealthy countries. The main costs are compliance and slower top speeds, which the bill's 70-mph option for trucks with modern braking technology tries to soften. On balance this was a well-supported safety rule, and its main flaw was not design but that it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up; it sat there until the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Johnny Isakson introduced the bill on December 10, 2019, joined by Senator Chris Coons as cosponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No further action was taken — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died in committee when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Trucking operators who would have had to cap their trucks at 65 mph are better off, since the mandate never took effect. Road users gain nothing from the outcome; the safety measure simply disappeared.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Trucking operators who never faced the 65 mph cap

for.name: Johnny Isakson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and named it after Cullum Owings, a young man killed in a truck crash.

for.name: Chris Coons
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the day it was introduced.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Roger Wicker
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill up for committee action during the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association
against.role: Trade group representing small trucking firms and independent truckers
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory truck speed limiters, arguing they create dangerous speed differences with faster car traffic and add costs to small operators.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican lead sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — but with only two senators behind it, no party bloc ever took a position in the record, and the bill died without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have capped truck speeds at 65 mph (70 mph with modern braking tech), slowing operations and adding compliance and certification costs. Large fleets that already limit their trucks would face little new burden, while small operators would bear more of the cost. The bill's own findings show a major driver survey with 64 percent support for the requirement.

industries.industry: Safety technology suppliers and truck manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would have created a guaranteed market for speed-limiting devices, automatic emergency braking, and adaptive cruise control on every new large truck, with federal performance standards for those systems.
